evidence_quotes.quote: The subject of this book is community-based water management in developing Asian countries, underlying social capital, and participatory approaches to water management initiated by rural and suburban residents in order to overcome the problem of the exclusion of vulnerable and small users from public water service.

In the case of PDAM Tirta Raharja (i.e., a state-owned enterprise), ownership belongs to Bandung Regency, whereas its coverage service includes Cimahi City and West Bandung Regency. Regarding water supply provision, the authority to determine production level and price is vested in the regent or mayor of the city.

The dependent variable is set to 1 for respondents who participate in CBWM (HIPPAM’s members and those who get water from public hydrants), and 0 for respondents who do not participate in CBWM or for those obtaining clean water from different access (PDAM, individual wells and others). From the estimation results, it might be concluded that the length of time living in the area and the price of monthly water usage are of significance to households making decisions about whether to join a community-based water supply system.

The most significant change in this neighborhood is a new understanding of the responsibilities associated with water management and the willingness to take responsibility for regular maintenance activities.

It then introduces a general theory of collective action and discusses how the general theory can be applied in the context of collective action in the management of water resources. It posits structuration and legitimation dynamics that can sustain collective action over a period of time. A set of propositions is deduced from the general theory for their empirical validation.
